extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics, literary critics, writers, and philosophers interested in principles of taste and the sublime
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for judging works of imagination and the elegant arts: defines 'taste', argues for common principles across humanity, and explains how senses, imagination, and judgment combine to produce good or bad taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is 'that faculty or those faculties of the mind, which are affected with, or which form a judgment of, the works of imagination and the elegant arts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition as the scope: taste concerns responses to imagination and elegant arts rather than a single simple idea. The author warns that strict definitions may circumscribe inquiry and that a definition should follow, not precede, investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of Common Principles of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There are principles of taste common to all mankind, enabling objective reasoning about the imagination and the arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue and judge works on the assumption of some universal standards (analogous to tests in reason). Without such common principles, laying down rules for taste would be futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Natural from Acquired Relish
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish between natural pleasures/pains of the senses and acquired tastes (e.g., tobacco, opium); natural pleasures form the stable standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, separate what is naturally pleasing (sweetness, light) from what habit, association, or drug effects have made agreeable. Acquired relish does not erase the original natural standards and should be treated as distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory Agreement as Foundation for Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the conformation of the senses is broadly the same in all men, sensations (light/dark, sweet/bitter, etc.) and the immediate pleasures/pains they produce provide a shared basis for taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat common sensory responses as primary evidence for judgments about beauty and pleasure. If someone genuinely cannot distinguish basic sensory qualities, this is treated as pathology (their organs are 'out of order').

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination is Derived from the Senses and Limited to Recombining Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination represents and recombines images received from the senses; it 'is incapable of producing anything absolutely new' and can only vary ideas received from the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because imagination is constrained to sensory material, evaluate imaginative works by (a) how they use sensory-derived images and (b) how effectively they recombine resemblance and sensation to move the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from Resemblance vs. Pleasure from Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination finds its chief pleasure in tracing resemblances (wit, metaphor), whereas the judgment takes pleasure in discovering differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess figurative and inventive writing by how striking and apt its resemblances are; recognize that readers are naturally more receptive to resemblance/creation of new images than to intellectual distinctions, which require more effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is Composite: Senses, Imagination, and Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called taste is partly perception of primary sensory pleasures, partly the secondary pleasures of the imagination, and partly the conclusions of the reasoning faculty concerning manners, passions, and human conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good aesthetic judgment must consider sensory effect, imaginative power, and moral/intellectual correctness (e.g., probability, manners). Deficiency in any of these dimensions weakens taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree Judgments Lack a Common Measure and Depend on Attention/Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities judged by degree (smoothness, polish, subtle colour shades) have no common external measure, so judgments about fine degrees rely on acuity of sense, attention, and practice rather than an objective scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer fine-grained disputes to specialists or those with practiced attention (e.g., a marble-polisher deciding polish). Expect disagreement where differences are minute; expertise matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and Experience Improve Critical Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical taste frequently depends on acquired knowledge (of art, nature, manners). Novices may be pleased by mere general resemblance; experts perceive deeper faults and finer merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works, take into account the evaluator's background knowledge. Examples: the shoemaker detects faulty shoes in a painting; the anatomist notices muscular inaccuracies. Training alters critical perception but does not imply superior natural taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Wrong or Vicious Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong taste arises from defects of judgment—natural weakness of understanding, ignorance, inattention, prejudice, rashness, levity, or obstinacy; lack of sensibility (blunt feelings) also produces poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose poor responses: determine whether they stem from insensibility (cannot be moved) or from poor judgment (misapplied reasoning or ignorance). Remedies differ: cultivate sensibility or provide directed education and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Imitation by Its Resemblance to the Original and Its Natural Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative works should be judged by (1) the pleasure they derive from the properties of the natural object and (2) the pleasure from their resemblance to that object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critiques of imitation (sculpture, painting, poetry), focus on fidelity of resemblance where appropriate and on whether the imitation produces the natural effect (sympathy, pleasure). Novices may value only general likeness; critical judgment requires knowledge of the original domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight and Taste Differ in Susceptibility to Habit and Association
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures of sight are less complicated and less altered by acquired associations than taste; tastes are more readily formed by habit and associations (food/drug examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when attributing value based on gustatory associations; visual beauty is comparatively more directly accessible as a standard. Account for cultural/habitual factors especially in evaluating taste-based pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and Representation of Passions Produce Immediate Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions represented in art (love, grief, fear, anger, joy) affect human minds by natural sympathy and are recognized justly and uniformly across people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representations of human passions primarily by their power to elicit natural sympathy; such representations are less liable to dispute provided they are naturally convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred Method of Teaching Taste: Investigative and Generative
rubrics_metrics.description: The best method of teaching taste approaches the method of investigation: it 'leads to the stock on which truths grew' and 'sets the reader himself in the track of invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructing about taste or critiquing to improve taste, favor methods that explain origins, principles, and processes rather than merely listing maxims; foster the learner's ability to discover and apply principles independently.
